[[File:Lush_bath_bombs.jpg|thumb|right]]
'''Nyūyokuzai''' (入浴剤) are substances added to bathwater during {{ill|Bathing|en|Bathing|qid=Q327651|lt=bathing}} in a {{ill|Furo|en|Furo|qid=Q2637646|lt=bathtub}}. These are prepared bath products, such as fragrant bath salts, intended for {{ill|Bathing|en|Bathing|qid=Q327651|lt=bathing}}.<ref name="osaka">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.customs.go.jp/osaka/toukei/pdf/tokushu_201004.pdf|title=入浴剤の輸入|publisher=大阪税関|accessdate=2019-10-20}}</ref>
They come in various forms, including {{ill|Solid|en|Solid|qid=Q11438|lt=solids}}, {{ill|Powder|en|Powder|qid=Q2908004|lt=powders}} and {{ill|Liquid|en|Liquid|qid=Q11435|lt=liquids}}. Bath additives can be broadly categorized into three types: those derived from natural {{ill|Plant|en|Plant|qid=Q756|lt=plants}} or {{ill|Chinese herbology|en|Chinese herbology|qid=Q261503|lt=herbal medicines}}, extracts of {{ill|Onsen|ar|أونسن|az|Onsen|bcl|Onsen|ca|Onsen|cs|Onsen|da|Onsen|de|Onsen|el|Όνσεν|eo|Onsen|es|Onsen|et|Onsen|eu|Onsen|fa|اونسن|fi|Onsen|fr|Onsen|he|אונסן|hu|Onszen|id|Onsen|it|Onsen|ja|温泉|km|អុនសេន|ko|일본의 온천|la|Onsen|lt|Onsenas|lv|Onsens|ms|Onsen|my|အွန်းဆန်း|nl|Onsen|nn|Onsen|no|Onsen|pl|Onsen|pt|Onsen|ro|Onsen|ru|Онсэн|simple|Onsen|sk|Onsen|sl|Onsen|sv|Onsen|ta|ஒன்சென்|th|อนเซ็ง|tl|Onsen|tr|Onsen|uk|Онсен|ur|اونسن|vi|Onsen|zh|日本溫泉|qid=Q655311|lt=hot spring water}} components, and inorganic {{ill|Mineral (nutrient)|ar|عنصر معدني (تغذية)|bn|খনিজ (পুষ্টি)|ca|Mineral (nutrient)|ce|Макродакъалгаш|ckb|کانزا (ماددەی خۆراکی)|cs|Minerály (výživa)|de|Mineralstoff|dv|ކާނާގައި ހިމެނޭ މަޢުދަންތައް|es|Mineral (nutriente)|et|Mineraaltoiteained|eu|Mineral (nutrizioa)|fa|مواد مغذی معدنی|fi|Kivennäisaine|fr|Nutriments minéraux|ga|Mianra (cothaitheach)|gl|Mineral (nutriente)|he|מינרל (תזונה)|hi|आहारीय खनिज|hr|Minerali (nutrijenti)|hu|Ásványi anyagok|id|Mineral (nutrisi)|inh|Биологега йийхкача, лоадам бола элементаш|it|Sali minerali|ja|ミネラル|ko|무기질|ky|Минералдык заттар|lt|Mineralinės medžiagos|lv|Minerālvielas|mk|Прехранбен минерал|ms|Zat galian|no|Mineral (ernæring)|or|ଖାଦ୍ୟ ଖଣିଜ ଲବଣ|pa|ਖ਼ੁਰਾਕੀ ਤੱਤ|pl|Biologiczne znaczenie pierwiastków|pt|Sais minerais|ru|Биологически значимые элементы|sh|Dijetetski minerali|simple|Dietary mineral|sk|Minerálna látka (výživa)|sr|Dijetetski mineral|sv|Mineraler (kost)|ta|கனிமம் (ஊட்டச்சத்து)|th|เกลือแร่|tr|Mineral (besin)|tt|Минерал матдәләр|tyv|Минералдыг бүдүмелдер|uk|Мінерали (поживні речовини)|vi|Khoáng chất (dinh dưỡng)|wuu|矿物质|xh|Imineral ekukutya|zh|礦物質|zh_yue|礦物質|qid=Q189598}} compounds. Combinations of these types are also available.
In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}}, bath additives are regulated as either {{ill|Cosmetics|en|Cosmetics|qid=Q131207|lt=cosmetics}} (bathing cosmetics), {{ill|quasi-drug|ja|医薬部外品|qid=Q11404705}}, or {{ill|Medication|en|Medication|qid=Q12140|lt=pharmaceuticals}}. Most products on the market are classified as quasi-drugs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jbia.org/safety6.html|title=日本浴用剤工業会|publisher=日本浴用剤工業会}}</ref> Quasi-drugs are legally permitted to display effects and efficacy claims similar to those of pharmaceuticals.
==Origin==
The history of bath additives dates back thousands of years across various regions. Around 2700 years {{ill|Ante Christum natum|en|Ante Christum natum|qid=Q28200|lt=Before the Common Era}}, texts from {{ill|China (region)|de|China|ja|中国|2=ja|3=中国|lt=China|zh|中国|2=ja|3=中国|lt=China|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q29520}} described multiple types of salts along with extraction and usage methods. The ancient Greek physician {{ill|Hippocrates|en|Hippocrates|qid=Q5264|lt=Hippocrates}} also immersed patients in seawater to treat various ailments and advocated the use of saltwater to his fellow healers.
Japan, a country renowned for its abundant hot springs, traces the origins of bath additives to therapeutic baths using natural spring water and medicinal plants.<ref name="osaka"/><ref>{{Citation|title=入浴剤の現状と展望|doi=10.11227/seikisho.56.121|publisher=日本生気象学会|date=2020-02-20|accessdate=2021-10-09|language=ja}}</ref>
===Derived from Plants and Herbal Medicines===
In ancient Egypt, people bathed with fragrant oils and flowers. In ancient Mexico, descriptions record people of all classes bathing daily with medicinal {{ill|Medicinal plants|en|Medicinal plants|qid=Q188840|lt=herbs}} for therapeutic purposes.<ref name="autogenerated1">{{cite web|title=…|language=es|url=http://148.206.53.231/UAMI11028.PDF|accessdate=2012-12-18}}</ref>
In Japan, medicinal plant baths ({{ill|herbal baths|de|Kräuterbäder|ja|薬湯|zh|药汤|qid=Q16496694}}) were popular, and during the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período diseases.<ref name="osaka"/> Traditional customs include adding iris on {{ill|Dragon Boat Festival|de|Tango-Fest|ja|端午の節句|zh|端午节|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 端午|comment=changed title based on {{ill|Yuzu|de|Yuzu-Frucht|ja|柚子|zh|柚子|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ユズ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q867776}} on {{ill|Winter solstice|en|Winter solstice|qid=Q207932|lt=Winter Solstice}} for {{ill|Yuzu bath|en|Yuzu bath|qid=Q11533980|lt=yuzu baths}}.<ref name="osaka"/> The “Five Woods and Eight Grasses Bath” described in {{ill|Yojokun|de|Yōjōkun|ja|養生訓|zh|养生训|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11666861}} by {{ill|Kaibara Ekken|en|Kaibara Ekken|qid=Q1721396|lt=Kaibara Ekiken}} lists plants such as [[:en:Mulberry|mulberry]], {{ill|Elm|de|Ulme|ja|楡|zh|榆|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ニレ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q131113}}, {{ill|Paulownia tomentosa|de|Kaiserbaum|ja|桐|zh|泡桐|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to キリ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q157393}}, iris, and {{ill|Lonicera japonica|de|Geißblatt|ja|忍冬|zh|忍冬|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to スイカズラ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q161083}}.<ref name="osaka"/> Bath specialties at places like {{ill|Daigo Onsen|de|Daigo-Onsen|ja|大子温泉|zh|大子温泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11434220}} may also include local fruits such as apples. By the mid-{{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} these medicinal herbs were packaged in cloth bags as commercial products.<ref name="osaka"/>
===Derived from Hot Spring Components===
Since the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, powdered forms of natural spring components have been commercialized.<ref name="osaka"/> A representative example is {{ill|Sinter|de|Thermalwasserablagerungen|ja|湯の花|lt=Yunohana|zh|汤之花|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563426}}. Adding these deposits to baths allows people far from springs to enjoy their benefits. These deposits are collected from {{ill|Yubatake|de|Onsen-Felder|ja|湯畑|2=ja|3=湯畑|4=zh|5=汤畑|6=de|7=Onsen-Felder|zh|汤畑|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563768}} or precipitated from alum-rich clay at the {{ill|Beppu Myōban Onsen|de|Beppu Myōban-Onsen|ja|別府の明礬温泉|zh|别府明矾温泉|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135503413}} in structures known as Sinter huts. Sulfurous or metal sulfide-rich deposits can damage tubs and should be verified before use. Some manufacturers process spring water from {{ill|Kusatsu Onsen|en|Kusatsu Onsen|qid=Q3137477|lt=Kusatsu Onsen}} or {{ill|Shiraoi Onsen|de|Shiraoi-Onsen|ja|白老温泉|zh|白老温泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11580321}} into liquid bath additives. Bath additives from Kusatsu are known for turning the water milky white and have been implicated in onsen misrepresentation scandals.
Products designed to mimic the effects of {{ill|radium springs|de|Radiumquellen|ja|放射能泉|zh|放射性温泉}} use processed {{ill|radium ore|de|Radiumerz|ja|ラジウム鉱石|zh|镭矿石|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135503414}} in mesh bags. Unlike hot spring deposits, these can be reused but are expensive and mostly used by {{ill|Sentō|en|Sentō|qid=Q1046648|lt=public bathhouses}}, {{ill|Super Sentō|de|Super-Sentōs|ja|スーパー銭湯|zh|超级公共浴场|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11313995}}, {{ill|Health land|de|Gesundheitslandschaften|ja|健康ランド|zh|健康乐园|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11387182}}, and inns. Some products hold {{ill|Medication|en|Medication|qid=Q12140|lt=pharmaceutical certification}}.
Bath additives marketed as “Onsen no Moto” claim to replicate specific hot spring compositions.
===Derived from Inorganic Mineral Compounds===
The most common domestic bath additives in Japan are made from stable, safe substances found in springs and emerged in the early {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era}}.<ref name="osaka"/> Initially aimed at users of public baths, since private tubs were rare.<ref name="osaka"/> From the 1960s economic boom and the proliferation of baths in public housing, by {{ill|1980|en|1980|qid=Q2439|lt=1980}}, the health trend drove market expansion.<ref name=":0"/> Carbon-dioxide-type and onsen-style bath additives as well as skincare-promoting products were launched around this time.<ref name=":0"/>
Powder and tablet forms account for over 80% of the market.<ref name=":0"/> Common ingredients in household powdered types include {{ill|Sodium sulfate|en|Sodium sulfate|qid=Q211737|lt=sodium sulfate}}, {{ill|Sodium bicarbonate|en|Sodium bicarbonate|qid=Q179731|lt=sodium bicarbonate}}, {{ill|Calcium sulfate|en|Calcium sulfate|qid=Q407258|lt=calcium sulfate}}, {{ill|Calcium carbonate|en|Calcium carbonate|qid=Q23767|lt=calcium carbonate}}, and titanium dioxide. Salts bond with skin proteins to form a film that reduces heat loss and enhances post-bathing warmth. Products containing {{ill|Sodium carbonate|en|Sodium carbonate|qid=Q190227|lt=sodium carbonate}} effervesce by releasing carbon dioxide ({{ill|Carbon ontuhlambili|qid=Q1997}}) when dissolved. Many products now include enzymes and plant extracts for beauty and health effects.<ref name=":0"/>
Some products use well-known onsen names purely for image; packaging often notes “This does not replicate onsen water.” True replication would damage tubs due to {{ill|Sulfur|en|Sulfur|qid=Q682|lt=sulfur}} content. Many products share the same base ingredients, differing only in dyes and fragrances.
Homemade bath additives can be made by mixing powders such as {{ill|Sodium sulfate|en|Sodium sulfate|qid=Q211737|lt=sodium sulfate}} and {{ill|Sodium bicarbonate|en|Sodium bicarbonate|qid=Q179731|lt=sodium bicarbonate}} with {{ill|Essential oil|en|Essential oil|qid=Q170885|lt=essential oils}} to create custom products.
==Ingredients of Bath Additives==
Homemade and additive ingredients include:
===Liquid Bases===
{{ill|Milk|en|Milk|qid=Q8495|lt=milk}}, {{ill|Soy milk|en|Soy milk|qid=Q192199|lt=soy milk}}, {{ill|Alcoholic beverage|en|Alcoholic beverage|qid=Q154|lt=alcohol}} (e.g., {{ill|Wine|en|Wine|qid=Q282|lt=wine}}), {{ill|Tea|en|Tea|qid=Q6097|lt=tea}}, {{ill|Lotion|en|Lotion|qid=Q1871151|lt=lotions}}, {{ill|rice water|de|Reiswasser|ja|とぎ汁|zh|淘米水|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11273066}}, {{ill|Honey|en|Honey|qid=Q10987|lt=honey}}, baby oil, {{ill|Perfume|en|Perfume|qid=Q131746|lt=perfume}}, {{ill|fragrant oils|de|Duftöle|ja|香油|zh|香油|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18990705}}, {{ill|Vinegar|en|Vinegar|qid=Q41354|lt=vinegar}}, {{ill|Polyethylene glycol|en|Polyethylene glycol|qid=Q410083|lt=polyethylene glycol}}, {{ill|Methanol|en|Methanol|qid=Q14982|lt=methanol}} (methyl alcohol is not used in Japanese bath additives).
===Herbal Bases===
{{ill|Pericarp|de|Schalen|ja|果皮|zh|果皮|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q876445}} (e.g., {{ill|Apple|en|Apple|qid=Q89|lt=apple}}, {{ill|Lemon|en|Lemon|qid=Q500|lt=lemon}}), spices and {{ill|Chinese herbology|en|Chinese herbology|qid=Q261503|lt=herbal medicines}} (e.g., {{ill|Ginger|en|Ginger|qid=Q35625|lt=ginger}}, {{ill|Chili pepper|en|Chili pepper|qid=Q165199|lt=chili pepper}}), and {{ill|Herb|en|Herb|qid=Q207123|lt=herbs}} (e.g., {{ill|Perilla frutescens|en|Perilla frutescens|qid=Q1076038|lt=perilla}}, {{ill|Peppermint|en|Peppermint|qid=Q156037|lt=peppermint}}).
===Solid Bases===
{{ill|Salt|de|Kochsalz|ja|食塩|zh|食盐|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 塩|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11254}}, {{ill|Bath salts|en|Bath salts|qid=Q798972|lt=bath salts}}, {{ill|Sodium bicarbonate|de|Natron|ja|重曹|zh|小苏打|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 炭酸水素ナトリウム|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q179731}}, {{ill|Citric acid|en|Citric acid|qid=Q159683|lt=citric acid}}, and {{ill|Sinter|de|Thermalwasserablagerungen|ja|湯の花|lt=Yunohana|zh|汤之花|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563426}}.

==Merged second translation==

[[File:Lush_bath_bombs.jpg|thumb|right]]
'''Nyūyokuzai''' (入浴剤) are substances added to bathwater during {{ill|Bathing|en|Bathing|qid=Q327651|lt=bathing}} in a {{ill|Furo|en|Furo|qid=Q2637646|lt=bathtub}}. These are prepared bath products, such as fragrant bath salts, intended for {{ill|Bathing|en|Bathing|qid=Q327651|lt=bathing}}.<ref name="osaka">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.customs.go.jp/osaka/toukei/pdf/tokushu_201004.pdf|title=入浴剤の輸入|publisher=大阪税関|accessdate=2019-10-20}}</ref>
They come in various forms, including {{ill|Solid|en|Solid|qid=Q11438|lt=solids}}, {{ill|Powder|en|Powder|qid=Q2908004|lt=powders}} and {{ill|Liquid|en|Liquid|qid=Q11435|lt=liquids}}. Bath additives can be broadly categorized into three types: those derived from natural {{ill|Plant|en|Plant|qid=Q756|lt=plants}} or {{ill|Chinese herbology|en|Chinese herbology|qid=Q261503|lt=herbal medicines}}, extracts of {{ill|Onsen|ar|أونسن|az|Onsen|bcl|Onsen|ca|Onsen|cs|Onsen|da|Onsen|de|Onsen|el|Όνσεν|eo|Onsen|es|Onsen|et|Onsen|eu|Onsen|fa|اونسن|fi|Onsen|fr|Onsen|he|אונסן|hu|Onszen|id|Onsen|it|Onsen|ja|温泉|km|អុនសេន|ko|일본의 온천|la|Onsen|lt|Onsenas|lv|Onsens|ms|Onsen|my|အွန်းဆန်း|nl|Onsen|nn|Onsen|no|Onsen|pl|Onsen|pt|Onsen|ro|Onsen|ru|Онсэн|simple|Onsen|sk|Onsen|sl|Onsen|sv|Onsen|ta|ஒன்சென்|th|อนเซ็ง|tl|Onsen|tr|Onsen|uk|Онсен|ur|اونسن|vi|Onsen|zh|日本溫泉|qid=Q655311|lt=hot spring water}} components, and inorganic {{ill|Mineral (nutrient)|ar|عنصر معدني (تغذية)|bn|খনিজ (পুষ্টি)|ca|Mineral (nutrient)|ce|Макродакъалгаш|ckb|کانزا (ماددەی خۆراکی)|cs|Minerály (výživa)|de|Mineralstoff|dv|ކާނާގައި ހިމެނޭ މަޢުދަންތައް|es|Mineral (nutriente)|et|Mineraaltoiteained|eu|Mineral (nutrizioa)|fa|مواد مغذی معدنی|fi|Kivennäisaine|fr|Nutriments minéraux|ga|Mianra (cothaitheach)|gl|Mineral (nutriente)|he|מינרל (תזונה)|hi|आहारीय खनिज|hr|Minerali (nutrijenti)|hu|Ásványi anyagok|id|Mineral (nutrisi)|inh|Биологега йийхкача, лоадам бола элементаш|it|Sali minerali|ja|ミネラル|ko|무기질|ky|Минералдык заттар|lt|Mineralinės medžiagos|lv|Minerālvielas|mk|Прехранбен минерал|ms|Zat galian|no|Mineral (ernæring)|or|ଖାଦ୍ୟ ଖଣିଜ ଲବଣ|pa|ਖ਼ੁਰਾਕੀ ਤੱਤ|pl|Biologiczne znaczenie pierwiastków|pt|Sais minerais|ru|Биологически значимые элементы|sh|Dijetetski minerali|simple|Dietary mineral|sk|Minerálna látka (výživa)|sr|Dijetetski mineral|sv|Mineraler (kost)|ta|கனிமம் (ஊட்டச்சத்து)|th|เกลือแร่|tr|Mineral (besin)|tt|Минерал матдәләр|tyv|Минералдыг бүдүмелдер|uk|Мінерали (поживні речовини)|vi|Khoáng chất (dinh dưỡng)|wuu|矿物质|xh|Imineral ekukutya|zh|礦物質|zh_yue|礦物質|qid=Q189598}} compounds. Combinations of these types are also available.
In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}}, bath additives are regulated as either {{ill|Cosmetics|en|Cosmetics|qid=Q131207|lt=cosmetics}} (bathing cosmetics), {{ill|quasi-drug|ja|医薬部外品|qid=Q11404705}}, or {{ill|Medication|en|Medication|qid=Q12140|lt=pharmaceuticals}}. Most products on the market are classified as quasi-drugs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jbia.org/safety6.html|title=日本浴用剤工業会|publisher=日本浴用剤工業会}}</ref> Quasi-drugs are legally permitted to display effects and efficacy claims similar to those of pharmaceuticals.
==Origin==
The history of bath additives dates back thousands of years across various regions. Around 2700 years {{ill|Ante Christum natum|en|Ante Christum natum|qid=Q28200|lt=Before the Common Era}}, texts from {{ill|China (region)|de|China|ja|中国|2=ja|3=中国|lt=China|zh|中国|2=ja|3=中国|lt=China|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q29520}} described multiple types of salts along with extraction and usage methods. The ancient Greek physician {{ill|Hippocrates|en|Hippocrates|qid=Q5264|lt=Hippocrates}} also immersed patients in seawater to treat various ailments and advocated the use of saltwater to his fellow healers.
Japan, a country renowned for its abundant hot springs, traces the origins of bath additives to therapeutic baths using natural spring water and medicinal plants.<ref name="osaka"/><ref>{{Citation|title=入浴剤の現状と展望|doi=10.11227/seikisho.56.121|publisher=日本生気象学会|date=2020-02-20|accessdate=2021-10-09|language=ja}}</ref>
===Derived from Plants and Herbal Medicines===
In ancient Egypt, people bathed with fragrant oils and flowers. In ancient Mexico, descriptions record people of all classes bathing daily with medicinal {{ill|Medicinal plants|en|Medicinal plants|qid=Q188840|lt=herbs}} for therapeutic purposes.<ref name="autogenerated1">{{cite web|title=…|language=es|url=http://148.206.53.231/UAMI11028.PDF|accessdate=2012-12-18}}</ref>
In Japan, medicinal plant baths ({{ill|herbal baths|de|Kräuterbäder|ja|薬湯|zh|药汤|qid=Q16496694}}) were popular, and during the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada diseases.<ref name="osaka"/> Traditional customs include adding iris on {{ill|Dragon Boat Festival|de|Tango-Fest|ja|端午の節句|zh|端午节|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 端午|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1254268}} for {{ill|iris baths|de|Schwertlilienbäder|ja|菖蒲湯|zh|菖蒲浴|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11619955}} and adding {{ill|Yuzu|de|Yuzu-Frucht|ja|柚子|zh|柚子|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ユズ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q867776}} on {{ill|Winter solstice|en|Winter solstice|qid=Q207932|lt=Winter Solstice}} for {{ill|Yuzu bath|en|Yuzu bath|qid=Q11533980|lt=yuzu baths}}.<ref name="osaka"/> The “Five Woods and Eight Grasses Bath” described in {{ill|Yojokun|de|Yōjōkun|ja|養生訓|zh|养生训|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11666861}} by {{ill|Kaibara Ekken|en|Kaibara Ekken|qid=Q1721396|lt=Kaibara Ekiken}} lists plants such as [[:en:Mulberry|mulberry]], {{ill|Elm|de|Ulme|ja|楡|zh|榆|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ニレ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q131113}}, {{ill|Paulownia tomentosa|de|Kaiserbaum|ja|桐|zh|泡桐|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to キリ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q157393}}, iris, and {{ill|Lonicera japonica|de|Geißblatt|ja|忍冬|zh|忍冬|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to スイカズラ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q161083}}.<ref name="osaka"/> Bath specialties at places like {{ill|Daigo Onsen|de|Daigo-Onsen|ja|大子温泉|zh|大子温泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11434220}} may also include local fruits such as apples. By the mid-{{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} these medicinal herbs were packaged in cloth bags as commercial products.<ref name="osaka"/>
===Derived from Hot Spring Components===
Since the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, powdered forms of natural spring components have been commercialized.<ref name="osaka"/> A representative example is {{ill|Sinter|de|Thermalwasserablagerungen|ja|湯の花|lt=Yunohana|zh|汤之花|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563426}}. Adding these deposits to baths allows people far from springs to enjoy their benefits. These deposits are collected from {{ill|Yubatake|de|Onsen-Felder|ja|湯畑|2=ja|3=湯畑|4=zh|5=汤畑|6=de|7=Onsen-Felder|zh|汤畑|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563768}} or precipitated from alum-rich clay at the {{ill|Beppu Myōban Onsen|de|Beppu Myōban-Onsen|ja|別府の明礬温泉|zh|别府明矾温泉|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135503413}} in structures known as Sinter huts. Sulfurous or metal sulfide-rich deposits can damage tubs and should be verified before use. Some manufacturers process spring water from {{ill|Kusatsu Onsen|en|Kusatsu Onsen|qid=Q3137477|lt=Kusatsu Onsen}} or {{ill|Shiraoi Onsen|de|Shiraoi-Onsen|ja|白老温泉|zh|白老温泉|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11580321}} into liquid bath additives. Bath additives from Kusatsu are known for turning the water milky white and have been implicated in onsen misrepresentation scandals.
Products designed to mimic the effects of {{ill|radium springs|de|Radiumquellen|ja|放射能泉|zh|放射性温泉}} use processed {{ill|radium ore|de|Radiumerz|ja|ラジウム鉱石|zh|镭矿石|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135503414}} in mesh bags. Unlike hot spring deposits, these can be reused but are expensive and mostly used by {{ill|Sentō|en|Sentō|qid=Q1046648|lt=public bathhouses}}, {{ill|Super Sentō|de|Super-Sentōs|ja|スーパー銭湯|zh|超级公共浴场|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11313995}}, {{ill|Health land|de|Gesundheitslandschaften|ja|健康ランド|zh|健康乐园|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11387182}}, and inns. Some products hold {{ill|Medication|en|Medication|qid=Q12140|lt=pharmaceutical certification}}.
Bath additives marketed as “Onsen no Moto” claim to replicate specific hot spring compositions.
===Derived from Inorganic Mineral Compounds===
The most common domestic bath additives in Japan are made from stable, safe substances found in springs and emerged in the early {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|qid=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era}}.<ref name="osaka"/> Initially aimed at users of public baths, since private tubs were rare.<ref name="osaka"/> From the 1960s economic boom and the proliferation of baths in public housing, by {{ill|1980|en|1980|qid=Q2439|lt=1980}}, the health trend drove market expansion.<ref name=":0"/> Carbon-dioxide-type and onsen-style bath additives as well as skincare-promoting products were launched around this time.<ref name=":0"/>
Powder and tablet forms account for over 80% of the market.<ref name=":0"/> Common ingredients in household powdered types include {{ill|Sodium sulfate|en|Sodium sulfate|qid=Q211737|lt=sodium sulfate}}, {{ill|Sodium bicarbonate|en|Sodium bicarbonate|qid=Q179731|lt=sodium bicarbonate}}, {{ill|Calcium sulfate|en|Calcium sulfate|qid=Q407258|lt=calcium sulfate}}, {{ill|Calcium carbonate|en|Calcium carbonate|qid=Q23767|lt=calcium carbonate}}, and titanium dioxide. Salts bond with skin proteins to form a film that reduces heat loss and enhances post-bathing warmth. Products containing {{ill|Sodium carbonate|en|Sodium carbonate|qid=Q190227|lt=sodium carbonate}} effervesce by releasing carbon dioxide ({{ill|Carbon ontuhlambili|qid=Q1997}}) when dissolved. Many products now include enzymes and plant extracts for beauty and health effects.<ref name=":0"/>
Some products use well-known onsen names purely for image; packaging often notes “This does not replicate onsen water.” True replication would damage tubs due to {{ill|Sulfur|en|Sulfur|qid=Q682|lt=sulfur}} content. Many products share the same base ingredients, differing only in dyes and fragrances.
Homemade bath additives can be made by mixing powders such as {{ill|Sodium sulfate|en|Sodium sulfate|qid=Q211737|lt=sodium sulfate}} and {{ill|Sodium bicarbonate|en|Sodium bicarbonate|qid=Q179731|lt=sodium bicarbonate}} with {{ill|Essential oil|en|Essential oil|qid=Q170885|lt=essential oils}} to create custom products.
==Ingredients of Bath Additives==
Homemade and additive ingredients include:
===Liquid Bases===
{{ill|Milk|en|Milk|qid=Q8495|lt=milk}}, {{ill|Soy milk|en|Soy milk|qid=Q192199|lt=soy milk}}, {{ill|Alcoholic beverage|en|Alcoholic beverage|qid=Q154|lt=alcohol}} (e.g., {{ill|Wine|en|Wine|qid=Q282|lt=wine}}), {{ill|Tea|en|Tea|qid=Q6097|lt=tea}}, {{ill|Lotion|en|Lotion|qid=Q1871151|lt=lotions}}, {{ill|rice water|de|Reiswasser|ja|とぎ汁|zh|淘米水|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11273066}}, {{ill|Honey|en|Honey|qid=Q10987|lt=honey}}, baby oil, {{ill|Perfume|en|Perfume|qid=Q131746|lt=perfume}}, {{ill|fragrant oils|de|Duftöle|ja|香油|zh|香油|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18990705}}, {{ill|Vinegar|en|Vinegar|qid=Q41354|lt=vinegar}}, {{ill|Polyethylene glycol|en|Polyethylene glycol|qid=Q410083|lt=polyethylene glycol}}, {{ill|Methanol|en|Methanol|qid=Q14982|lt=methanol}} (methyl alcohol is not used in Japanese bath additives).
===Herbal Bases===
{{ill|Pericarp|de|Schalen|ja|果皮|zh|果皮|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q876445}} (e.g., {{ill|Apple|en|Apple|qid=Q89|lt=apple}}, {{ill|Lemon|en|Lemon|qid=Q500|lt=lemon}}), spices and {{ill|Chinese herbology|en|Chinese herbology|qid=Q261503|lt=herbal medicines}} (e.g., {{ill|Ginger|en|Ginger|qid=Q35625|lt=ginger}}, {{ill|Chili pepper|en|Chili pepper|qid=Q165199|lt=chili pepper}}), and {{ill|Herb|en|Herb|qid=Q207123|lt=herbs}} (e.g., {{ill|Perilla frutescens|en|Perilla frutescens|qid=Q1076038|lt=perilla}}, {{ill|Peppermint|en|Peppermint|qid=Q156037|lt=peppermint}}).
===Solid Bases===
{{ill|Salt|de|Kochsalz|ja|食塩|zh|食盐|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 塩|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11254}}, {{ill|Bath salts|en|Bath salts|qid=Q798972|lt=bath salts}}, {{ill|Sodium bicarbonate|de|Natron|ja|重曹|zh|小苏打|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 炭酸水素ナトリウム|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q179731}}, {{ill|Citric acid|en|Citric acid|qid=Q159683|lt=citric acid}}, and {{ill|Sinter|de|Thermalwasserablagerungen|ja|湯の花|lt=Yunohana|zh|汤之花|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11563426}}.
